questions.q: Define "network topology" and name the five standard topologies covered in CBSE Class 11.
questions.a: Network topology is the arrangement of nodes and links in a network, defining data flow paths. The five standard topologies are Bus, Star, Ring, Mesh, and Tree. A wrong answer (e.g., listing "Hybrid" or "Wireless" as standard, or confusing topology with network types like LAN/MAN) reveals the student is mixing up network classification (scale) with topology (structure), or relying on informal knowledge instead of syllabus-defined categories.

questions.q: In a Star topology, all nodes connect to a central device. Explain why a single cable failure affects only one node, whereas in Bus topology the same failure can bring down the entire network.
questions.a: In Star, each node has a dedicated point-to-point link to the central hub/switch; a break isolates only that link. In Bus, all nodes share a single backbone cable; a break anywhere splits the backbone, leaving all nodes on both segments without a complete path to each other. A wrong answer (e.g., "Star has more cables so it's safer") shows the student memorizes "Star is robust" without understanding the structural reason: dedicated links vs. shared medium.

questions.q: A small startup has 8 computers and wants to minimize cabling cost while allowing easy addition of new devices. They do not have a dedicated server room. Which topology would you recommend? Justify with two reasons.
questions.a: Recommend Bus topology. Reason 1: Uses least cable (single backbone with drop lines), minimizing cost for 8 nodes. Reason 2: Adding a new node only requires a drop line and tap connector, no re-cabling of existing nodes. A wrong answer (e.g., recommending Star for "reliability") ignores the explicit constraints: cost minimization and no central device infrastructure. This reveals inability to match topology characteristics to scenario constraints.

questions.q: Compare Mesh and Tree topologies on: (a) number of links required for n nodes, (b) fault tolerance, (c) typical use case. Present as a table.
questions.a:
| Parameter | Mesh (Full) | Tree |
|-----------|-------------|------|
| Links for n nodes | n(n-1)/2 | n-1 (hierarchical) |
| Fault Tolerance | Very high (multiple paths) | Low (failure of parent link isolates subtree) |
| Typical Use | Critical backbone, WAN links, military | Large corporate LANs, ISP networks |
A wrong answer (e.g., claiming Tree has high fault tolerance) shows confusion between Tree's hierarchical redundancy (multiple children) and actual path redundancy. Tree has no alternative paths; Mesh does.

questions.q: Critique this statement: "Ring topology is obsolete because Star topology is better in every way." Provide two counter-arguments where Ring might still be preferred.
questions.a: Counter-argument 1: Ring (especially Token Ring / FDDI) provides deterministic access and guaranteed bandwidth without collisions, which is superior for real-time applications (e.g., industrial control) compared to Ethernet Star (CSMA/CD) under heavy load. Counter-argument 2: Ring requires less cable than Star for the same number of nodes arranged in a line (e.g., factory floor machines), reducing installation cost. A wrong answer (e.g., "Ring is never used") shows lack of awareness of niche applications and historical context; the statement is an overgeneralization.

questions.q: Design a network topology for a university campus with 5 buildings (each with 50 computers) connected to a central admin block. The admin block must monitor all traffic. Draw the topology, label all components, and explain why your choice balances cost, scalability, and monitoring.
questions.a: Use Tree topology: Admin block as root (central switch), each building as a child segment (with its own Star topology switch connecting 50 PCs), linked via fiber backbone. Admin root switch connects to all building switches. This allows: (1) Scalability — add buildings by connecting new switch to root; (2) Cost — each building uses Star internally (standard), backbone uses minimal fiber links; (3) Monitoring — admin root sees all inter-building traffic. A poor answer (e.g., Mesh between all buildings) ignores cost and over-engineers for a hierarchical organization.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Network topology refers to the physical or logical ______ of nodes (computers, servers, peripherals) and the connections (links) between them in a computer network, defining how data flows between devices.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are setting up a computer lab for 20 ______ in your school.
What is Network topology? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Network topology refers to the physical or logical arrangement of nodes (computers, servers, peripherals) and the connections (links) between them in a computer network, defining how data flows between devices.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you are setting up a computer lab for ______ computers in your school.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Network topology?
questions.a: Students often believe "Star topology requires a server at the center." They confuse the central connecting device (hub/switch) with a server (which provides services like file, print, authentication).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) Draw and label all five topologies (Bus, Star, Ring, Mesh, Tree) with correct terminology for nodes, links, backbone, central hub/switch, and terminators; (2) Compare them across at least four parameters (cost, fault tolerance, ease of troubleshooting, scalability, cable length) in a structured table; (3).
